did_you_know.text: Did you know? Ezekiel is commanded to turn his face toward the south, preach against it, and prophesy against the “forest of the field”—a prophetic reference to the land of Israel through the image of a forest.
Did you know? The fire in the prophecy is described as consuming both green wood and dry wood, and it cannot be extinguished; this emphasizes the extent and intensity of the destruction.
Did you know? The people regard Ezekiel’s words as nothing more than a parable—“Is he not merely telling parables?”—even though the prophet is describing an actual calamity that is about to come.
Did you know? The prophecy becomes explicit: the LORD’s sword will come out of its sheath and cut off both the righteous and the wicked from the land, and the sword will be directed against everyone.
Did you know? Ezekiel is told to sigh before the people, and his sigh serves as a sign of the disaster that will cause hearts to melt, hands to grow weak, and every spirit to faint.
Did you know? The sword is described twice as the “sword, sword,” and it is sharpened and polished to carry out a slaughter and gleam in preparation for its task.
Did you know? Ezekiel is commanded to cry out and strike his thigh with his hand, expressing mourning over the sword that will come against the people and the princes of Israel.
Did you know? The king of Babylon stands at the fork of two roads and uses divination to decide where to send his army: he casts arrows, consults the teraphim, and examines the liver.

Did you know? The prophecy describes the removal of the turban and the taking off of the crown, symbolizing the downfall of the ruling order and a reversal of social status: the lowly will be exalted and the exalted will be humbled.

Did you know? The prophecy of calamity against the Ammonites ends with images of fire, blood, and oblivion: “You will not be remembered,” and everything is declared as the conclusion to the proclamation, “I, the LORD, have spoken.”
